We learn y = w x using one example: x = 2 and y = 10. So the best w is 5.

The loss is (2w - 10) squared. The slope is 4 x (2w - 10). We start at w = 0.

Explanation

New w = old w - learning rate x slope.

Learning rate 0.05: the first slope is -40, so w becomes 2. The next slope is -24, so w becomes 3.2. It gets closer to 5.

Learning rate 0.25: the first slope is -40, so w becomes 10. The next slope is +40, so w goes back to 0.

With the large rate, w jumps from one side to the other and does not get closer. A rate that works for one problem can be too large for another.

6.3Batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent

To compute the gradient of the average loss, in principle you must look at every training example. For millions of examples that is slow. The three variants differ in how much data is used for each step.

Batch GDStochastic GD (SGD)Mini-batch GD
Data per updatethe whole training setone examplea small group (for example 32 or 64)
Cost of one updatehighvery lowlow
Updates per passoneas many as examplesexamples / batch size
Path to the minimumsmooth, directnoisy, zig-zagfairly smooth
Memoryhighlowmoderate
Best forsmall datasetshuge data, online learning; the noise can help escape poor local minimastandard choice in deep learning

Mini-batch is the compromise that wins. It gives frequent updates (so learning starts quickly), a steadier direction than a single example, and it maps well onto GPUs, which process a block of examples in parallel.

We want the opinion of 60,000 people before each decision. We can ask everyone, one person, or a random group of 64 people.

Explanation

If we ask everyone, the answer is reliable, but it takes a long time.

If we ask one person, it is fast, but that opinion can be very different from the others.

A group of 64 is a middle way. It is much faster than everyone and usually steadier than one person.

A mini-batch works in a similar way. Also, a GPU can process many examples at the same time.

Epoch and iteration

One epoch is one complete pass through the entire training set. One iteration is one weight update on one batch. With 10,000 images and a batch size of 100, one epoch has 100 iterations. Training for 10 epochs means the model has seen every image 10 times. The loss normally falls as epochs go by, and we stop when it stops improving.

We have 60,000 training images. One mini-batch has 64 images. We count the weight updates in one epoch (one full pass over the data).

Explanation

Batch gradient descent uses all images together: 1 update.

Stochastic gradient descent uses one image at a time: 60,000 updates.

Mini-batch: 60,000 / 64 = 937.5. The images that remain form a smaller last batch, so there are 938 updates.

All three methods use every image once. They differ in how many images they use for each update.

6.4The end-to-end machine learning workflow

Every ML project, from a college assignment to a company product, follows the same seven steps. Knowing the order, and the reason for each step, is a frequent exam question.

  1. Collect data from files, databases, sensors or APIs. This is the foundation.
  2. Prepare data: clean it, handle missing values, engineer and scale features, then split into training, validation and test sets. Usually the longest step.
  3. Choose a model suited to the problem (classification or regression), the amount of data and the need to explain results.
  4. Train the model on the training data so it learns its parameters.
  5. Evaluate it on unseen data with suitable metrics to see how well it generalises.
  6. Tune hyperparameters using the validation set, then retrain and re-evaluate. Repeat until satisfied.
  7. Predict and deploy: put the final model into real use on new data, and keep monitoring it, because real-world data changes over time.

Why is the order fixed? Cleaning must come before training (or the model learns garbage). Splitting must come before tuning (or the test set leaks). Evaluation must use data the model has not trained on (or the score is meaningless). Each step protects the honesty of the next.

A teacher gives students the real exam paper for practice. Later, the teacher uses the same paper for the exam. The scores are high.

Explanation

The scores do not show whether students can answer new questions, because they saw these questions before.

A model has the same problem if test data affects its training or settings.

So split the data early. Learn fill-in and scaling values from the training data. Choose settings with the validation data. Use the test data last.

A school wants to predict whether a student will pass.

1. Collect: get past student records.

2. Prepare: split the data and fill the blanks.

3. Choose: select logistic regression, a model for yes or no answers.

4. Train: let the model learn from the training data.

5. Evaluate: test it on students that it did not see.

6. Tune: try other settings with the validation data.

7. Use: predict for this year and compare with the real results.

Explanation

The answer is pass or fail, so this is classification.

Find fill-in values and scaling values from the training data only. Then no test information enters training.

The syllabus or the students can change. For this reason, step 7 includes regular review of the results.

6.5Exam questions and model answers: Chapter 6

Q1. What is the concept of a gradient?

The gradient of a function is a vector of its slopes with respect to each variable; it points in the direction of steepest increase. For a loss function, the gradient with respect to the weights shows how the loss changes when each weight is changed slightly. Moving against the gradient reduces the loss.

Q2. How does the gradient descent algorithm work?

It is an iterative optimisation method. Start from random parameters, compute the gradient of the loss at the current point, move a small step in the opposite direction (downhill), and repeat until the gradient is near zero, which is a minimum of the loss. The step size is controlled by the learning rate.

Q3. What is the weight update rule in gradient descent?

w_new = w_old - learning rate x (dLoss/dw). It is applied to every weight and bias. The minus sign makes the step go downhill, and the learning rate scales the step.

Q4. What is the role of the learning rate?

It controls the step size. If too small, training is very slow and may get stuck; if too large, the updates overshoot the minimum and the loss may oscillate or diverge. A well-chosen value gives fast, stable convergence.

Q5. Compare batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent.

Batch uses the whole dataset for each update: smooth but slow and memory-heavy. Stochastic uses one example per update: fast but noisy. Mini-batch uses a small group: a balance of speed and stability, and it is the standard in deep learning.

Q6. Define loss function, learning rate and epoch.

Loss function: a function measuring the discrepancy between predictions and true values that training tries to minimise. Learning rate: the hyperparameter (typically 0.0001 to 0.1) controlling the size of weight updates. Epoch: one complete pass of the training algorithm over the whole training dataset.

Q7. Describe an end-to-end ML workflow.

Collect data; prepare it (clean, engineer and scale features, split); choose a model; train; evaluate on unseen data; tune hyperparameters with the validation set; and finally deploy the model to predict on new data.

Q8. How does data quality affect ML models?

Data quality is the most important factor in performance: poor data gives inaccurate predictions, biased and unfair outcomes, poor generalisation, and wasted time. This is the "garbage in, garbage out" principle, and the reason cleaning takes most of the effort in a project.

Chapter 7

Unsupervised Learning Algorithms

Finding groups and structure in data that has no labels.

7.1K-Means clustering

K-Means is the standard method for grouping data. It repeatedly asks two simple questions: "which centre is each point closest to?" and "where is the middle of each group?".

The algorithm

  1. Choose K, the number of clusters you want, and pick K points at random as the starting centres (centroids).
  2. Assignment step: measure the distance from every point to every centroid (usually straight-line Euclidean distance), and put each point in the cluster of its nearest centroid.
  3. Update step: move each centroid to the average position of all the points now in its cluster.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the assignments stop changing.

Look at the figure. The random centres in panel 1 start in poor places. After the first assignment, each point joins the closer centre and the centres move to the middle of their groups (panel 2). In the next round two points change group, the centres move again, and in panel 3 nothing changes any more: the clusters have settled.

Why does it converge? Each assignment step makes every point closer (or equal) to its own centre, and each update step puts the centre exactly at the average of its points, which is the position that minimises the total squared distance. Since the total distance can only go down and there are finitely many groupings, the process must stop.

Use the marks 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12 and the first centers 2 and 3. For each point, square its distance to its center. Then add the squares.

Explanation

Give each point its nearest first center: the total is 195.

Move the centers to the group averages, 2 and 8: the total falls to 70.

Give each point its nearest center again: the total falls to 34.

Move the centers to 3 and 11: the total falls to 4.

These two steps never make the total larger. There is a limited number of possible groups, so with a fixed rule for ties, the method stops. The final groups are not always the best ones.

Practical points

  • K is a hyperparameter. A common way to choose it is the elbow method: run K-Means for K = 1, 2, 3, ... and plot the total within-cluster distance. It drops sharply at first and then flattens; the bend (the "elbow") suggests a sensible K.
  • The result depends on the random starting points, so the algorithm is usually run several times.
  • It uses distances, so features should be scaled.
  • It works best for round, similar-sized clusters and is thrown off by outliers.

Example use: grouping customers by their purchasing behaviour into segments such as "bargain hunters" and "premium buyers", so each group gets a suitable offer.

Make 2 groups from the marks 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12. Choose 2 and 3 as the first centers.

Explanation

Each mark joins the nearest center. Then each center moves to the average of its group.

Round 1: the groups are {2} and {3, 4, 10, 11, 12}. The new centers are 2 and 8.

Round 2: the mark 4 is 2 away from center 2, but 4 away from center 8. The groups become {2, 3, 4} and {10, 11, 12}. The new centers are 3 and 11.

Round 3: no mark changes its group, so we stop.

The first centers were poor, but the steps corrected them. With harder data, different first centers can give different groups.

7.2Hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN

Hierarchical clustering

Start with every point as its own cluster. Repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until only one remains. The merging history is drawn as a tree called a dendrogram; cutting the tree at a chosen height gives the clusters. Its advantage is that you do not need to decide K in advance, and you can see the structure at every level of detail.

DBSCAN

DBSCAN groups points that are densely packed together and labels isolated points as noise. It does not need K, can find clusters of any shape (even curved or ring-shaped, where K-Means fails), and handles outliers naturally. Its settings are how close points must be to count as neighbours and how many neighbours make a dense region.

Five points are on a line: 1, 2, 6, 7 and 20.

Explanation

Hierarchical clustering joins the closest groups first. Here, the gap between two groups means the gap between their nearest points.

First, it joins 1 with 2, and 6 with 7, because each gap is 1. Next, it joins these two groups (gap 4). Last, it adds 20 (gap 13).

If we stop before the last two joins, we get 3 groups. If we stop before only the last join, we get 2 groups.

DBSCAN looks for crowded areas. Use a radius of 1.5 and at least 2 points, and count the point itself.

DBSCAN finds {1, 2} and {6, 7}. The point 20 has no close neighbor, so DBSCAN marks it as noise.

7.3Dimensionality reduction: PCA and t-SNE

A dataset can have hundreds of features, many of them overlapping. Dimensionality reduction squeezes it into a few new features while keeping most of the information.

  • PCA (Principal Component Analysis) finds new axes, called principal components, along which the data varies most. The first component captures the largest variation, the second the next largest (at right angles to the first), and so on. Keeping only the first few components gives a compact description. Analogy: a 3D object casts a shadow; if you choose the best angle, the 2D shadow still shows the main shape.
  • t-SNE squeezes high-dimensional data into two or three dimensions purely for drawing pictures, placing similar points close together so clusters become visible.

Why reduce dimensions? Fewer features mean faster training, less overfitting, less storage, and the possibility of plotting the data to see what is going on. The price is that the new features are combinations of the old ones and harder to interpret.

A report has marks in 10 subjects for each student. We want one graph of the whole class.

Explanation

A flat graph has only 2 axes, but the data has 10 columns.

PCA makes 2 new values from the 10 marks. It chooses them to keep as much variation (differences in the data) as 2 straight axes can.

Now we can draw one point for each student.

Each new value mixes several subjects, so it is harder to explain. We also lose some information. Find how much variation the 2 values keep.

A table gives the height of each student two times: in centimeters and in inches.

Explanation

If you know one height, you can calculate the other. So the two columns repeat the same information.

On a graph, all the points lie on one straight line.

PCA makes a new axis along this line. This one axis keeps all the variation (differences between students). We can drop the second axis, which has almost none.

Real columns usually repeat each other only in part. Then we lose some information when we drop an axis.

7.4Exam questions and model answers: Chapter 7

Q1. Explain the logic of the K-Means clustering algorithm.

Choose the number of clusters K and select K random points as initial centroids. Then repeat two steps until assignments no longer change: (1) assignment: compute the distance from each data point to every centroid and assign the point to the nearest one; (2) update: recompute each centroid as the mean of the points assigned to it. The output is the final cluster of each point and the final centroids.

Q2. How do you choose K in K-Means?

K is a hyperparameter. The elbow method plots the within-cluster sum of squared distances against K and picks the K where the curve bends and stops dropping sharply. Domain knowledge also guides the choice.

Q3. List the main unsupervised learning techniques.

Clustering: K-Means, hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN. Dimensionality reduction: PCA and t-SNE. Association rule learning is also used for recommendations.

Q4. What is dimensionality reduction and why is it useful?

It reduces the number of features while preserving the important information. It speeds up training, reduces overfitting and storage, and allows high-dimensional data to be visualised.

Q5. Give use cases of unsupervised learning.

Customer segmentation, anomaly and fraud detection, recommendation by association, grouping similar images, topic modelling of documents, and PCA for dimensionality reduction.

Chapter 8

Neural Networks: The Foundations of Deep Learning

From a single artificial neuron to multi-layer networks, and how they learn through backpropagation.

8.1What is Deep Learning and why do we use it?

Deep Learning is machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. "Deep" refers to the number of layers. Each layer takes the output of the previous one and builds a slightly more abstract idea from it.

Recognising a face. The first layers detect tiny edges and dots. The next layers combine edges into shapes such as eyes and noses. The last layers combine those into a whole face. Nobody told the network to look for eyes: it discovered that this is a useful stepping stone.

Why deep learning instead of classic ML?

In classic ML a human must design the features first ("count the edges", "measure the colour"). This is hard for pictures, sound and language. A deep network learns the features itself, directly from raw pixels, audio or text, and it keeps improving as it is given more data. That is why it dominates these areas.

Key applications

AreaExamplesTypical network
Computer visionimage classification, object detection in self-driving cars, face recognitionCNN
Natural languagemachine translation, sentiment analysis, chatbots such as ChatGPTRNN, LSTM, Transformer
Predictive analyticsstock forecasting, fraud detection, disease diagnosis from structured datafeed-forward network, RNN

We want a computer to read the handwritten digit 7.

Classic ML: a person writes code to measure clues, such as the number of straight lines. The model learns from these clues.

Deep learning: we give the network the image pixels and the correct digit.

Explanation

In classic ML, a person chooses the clues. If someone writes a 7 in an unusual way, the clues can fail.

In deep learning, the network learns useful clues during training.

To do this, it usually needs more data and more computer power. For small tables of data, classic ML is often a good choice.

8.2The biological neuron and the artificial neuron

Artificial neural networks are loosely inspired by the brain. A brain cell receives signals through branches, adds them up, and if the total is strong enough it "fires" a signal onward. The artificial version copies this idea as a tiny piece of arithmetic.

Biological neuronArtificial neuron
Dendrites receive signals from other neuronsInputs x1, x2, ..., xn receive numbers
Synapses have different strengths, which change as we learnWeights w: how much each input matters; they are what gets learned
The cell body (soma) combines the incoming signalsA weighted sum of inputs plus a bias
It fires only if a threshold is reachedAn activation function decides the output
The axon carries the signal to other neuronsThe output is passed to the next layer
About 86 billion neurons with trillions of connections: extremely complexA simple mathematical function; networks have millions of them, still far fewer than a brain

The brain analogy is only loose inspiration. An artificial neuron is just a formula, and a neural network is just many of these formulas wired together. Do not expect it to work like a real brain.

One artificial neuron decides: "Take an umbrella?" For each input, 1 means yes.

Inputs: cloudy = 1, rain in the forecast = 1, travel by car = 1.

Weights: 1, 3 and -2. Bias: -1. The answer is yes if the sum is above 0.

Explanation

Multiply each input by its weight, and add the bias: 1 + 3 - 2 - 1 = 1.

The sum is above 0, so the answer is yes.

The forecast has the largest positive weight, so it pushes strongly toward yes. Travel by car has a negative weight, so it pushes toward no.

If there is no rain in the forecast, the sum is -2, and the answer is no.

8.3The perceptron: the building block

The perceptron is the simplest neural network: a single neuron that makes a yes/no decision. It is a linear classifier, meaning it separates two classes with a straight line (or flat plane).

output = f( w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + wn xn + b )

The four ingredients

  • Inputs (x): the features of one example.
  • Weights (w): one per input, saying how important that input is. A large positive weight pushes the neuron to fire (excitatory). A negative weight pushes against firing (inhibitory). A weight near zero means "ignore this input". Training changes the weights.
  • Bias (b): a constant added to the sum. It shifts the point at which the neuron fires, exactly like the intercept c in the line y = mx + c. Without a bias, the decision boundary would be forced to pass through the origin, which severely limits what the neuron can learn.
  • Activation function (f): converts the sum into the final output (step, sigmoid, ReLU).

AND gate. Choose w1 = 1, w2 = 1, bias b = -1.5, and the rule "output 1 if the sum is greater than 0".

x1x2sum = x1 + x2 - 1.5output
00-1.50
01-0.50
10-0.50
110.51

The neuron behaves as an AND gate. Notice the role of the bias: without it (b = 0), the input (1, 0) would give a sum of 1 and fire wrongly. The bias of -1.5 sets how much total evidence is needed before the neuron fires. In a real problem nobody picks these numbers by hand; the learning algorithm finds them from data.

How a perceptron learns

It learns by correcting its mistakes. For each training example it makes a prediction, compares it with the true answer, and if it was wrong it nudges the weights: if it said 0 but the answer was 1, the weights of the active inputs go up so the sum is larger next time; if it said 1 but the answer was 0, they go down. This is written out as a program in the last chapter.

An OR gate gives 1 if at least one input is 1. Use w1 = 1, w2 = 1 and bias = -0.5. The output is 1 if the sum is above 0.

Explanation

Inputs (0, 0): the sum is -0.5, so the output is 0.

Inputs (0, 1) or (1, 0): the sum is 0.5, so the output is 1.

Inputs (1, 1): the sum is 1.5, so the output is 1.

The AND gate in this lesson has the same weights, but its bias is -1.5. So AND needs both inputs, but OR needs only one. The bias controls how easily the neuron gives 1.

8.4Why one neuron is not enough: the XOR problem

A single perceptron draws one straight line. That is enough for AND, but some problems cannot be split by any single line. The classic example is XOR ("exclusive or"), which outputs 1 only when the two inputs are different.

The fix is to add a hidden layer. One hidden neuron can learn "at least one input is on" and another "both inputs are on"; the output neuron then combines them as "the first but not the second". Several neurons together draw several lines and combine them into curved or complicated boundaries. This is the reason we need multi-layer (deep) networks.

XOR gives 1 only when the two inputs are different. We use three neurons. Each one gives 1 if its sum is above 0.

Neuron h1 uses x1 + x2 - 0.5. This answers: is at least one input 1?

Neuron h2 uses x1 + x2 - 1.5. This answers: are both inputs 1?

The output neuron uses h1 - h2 - 0.5.

Explanation

Inputs (0, 0): h1 = 0 and h2 = 0, so the output is 0.

Inputs (0, 1) or (1, 0): h1 = 1 and h2 = 0, so the output is 1.

Inputs (1, 1): h1 = 1 and h2 = 1, so the output is 0.

The last neuron means "at least one, but not both". The two hidden neurons turn the inputs into new facts that one final line can separate.

8.5Activation functions

After the neuron adds up its weighted inputs, the activation function transforms that sum into the neuron's output.

FunctionWhat it doesWhere it is used and its weakness
Stepoutputs 0 or 1 at a thresholdthe original perceptron; not smooth, so it cannot be trained by gradient descent
Sigmoidsquashes any number into the range 0 to 1output layer for yes/no problems, because the result reads as a probability. It flattens at both ends, so gradients become tiny (vanishing gradient)
Tanhsquashes into -1 to 1, centred on zerohidden layers in older networks and in RNNs; also flattens at the ends
ReLU f(z) = max(0, z)passes positive values unchanged and turns negative values to zerothe default for hidden layers: very cheap to compute and it does not flatten for positive values, so gradients survive. A neuron stuck outputting zero can stop learning
Softmaxturns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1output layer for many-class problems

Why do we need activation functions at all? Without them, every layer would just multiply and add, and stacking such steps gives another multiply-and-add. Two layers W2 (W1 x) collapse into a single layer (W2 W1) x. A hundred layers would learn nothing that one layer could not: only straight lines. A non-linear activation between layers breaks this, allowing the network to bend its decision boundary and learn curved, complicated patterns. A second job is to control the output range (for example squeezing into 0 to 1 for a probability).

Network A has no activation function: h = 2x + 1, then y = 3h - 4.

Network B uses ReLU: y = ReLU(x) + ReLU(-x).

Explanation

In network A, put the first formula into the second: y = 3(2x + 1) - 4 = 6x - 1. The two layers do the work of one straight line.

In network B, the inputs -3, 0 and 3 give the outputs 3, 0 and 3. The graph has a V shape.

One straight line cannot make a V shape. ReLU makes this bend possible.

Which one should I use?

  • Hidden layers: ReLU (the default).
  • Output layer, two classes: sigmoid. Many classes: softmax.
  • Output layer for regression: no activation, so the output can be any number.

Give the values -2, 0 and 2 to different activation functions.

Sigmoid gives 0.12, 0.50 and 0.88.

Tanh gives -0.96, 0 and 0.96.

ReLU gives 0, 0 and 2.

Softmax changes the list of scores (2, 1, 0) into 0.67, 0.24 and 0.09.

Explanation

Sigmoid gives values between 0 and 1.

Tanh gives values between -1 and 1, with 0 in the middle.

ReLU changes negative values to 0 and keeps positive values.

Softmax uses the whole list together. The highest score gets the largest share. Before rounding, the shares add to 1.

8.6Neural network architecture: layers, weights and biases

A single neuron is weak, but thousands arranged in layers can learn remarkable things. The standard arrangement is called a feed-forward network: information flows in one direction, from the input to the output, with no loops.

  • Input layer: one node per feature (three nodes for three features). It does no calculation; it only passes the data on.
  • Hidden layers: the layers between input and output. They do the learning, building more complex patterns layer by layer. "Deep" means many hidden layers.
  • Output layer: produces the prediction. A yes/no problem uses one node with sigmoid; a problem with ten classes uses ten nodes with softmax; a regression problem uses one node with no activation.
  • Weights and biases: every connection has a weight and every neuron has a bias. These are the parameters, and they are exactly what training adjusts.

Counting parameters. For a network with 3, 4 and 2 neurons in successive layers: weights = 3 x 4 + 4 x 2 = 20 and biases = 4 + 2 = 6, so 26 parameters. Real networks have millions or billions, which is why they need large datasets and GPUs.

Single-layer versus multi-layer

A single-layer network connects inputs straight to outputs, so it can only solve linearly separable problems. A multi-layer network has hidden layers and, together with non-linear activations, can learn complex relationships such as XOR.

A network has 4 inputs, 5 hidden neurons and 3 output neurons. Each neuron connects to all values in the layer before it.

Explanation

Weights from the inputs to the hidden layer: 4 x 5 = 20.

Weights from the hidden layer to the output layer: 5 x 3 = 15.

Each hidden neuron and each output neuron has one bias: 5 + 3 = 8. Inputs have no bias.

Total: 20 + 15 + 8 = 43 parameters.

8.7Forward propagation

Forward propagation (the forward pass) is how a network produces a prediction: the input is pushed through the layers, one after another.

At each layer: (1) take the outputs of the previous layer, (2) for each neuron compute the weighted sum plus bias, (3) apply the activation function, (4) hand the results to the next layer. When the output layer is reached, we have the prediction.

Why matrix multiplication is central

A layer has many neurons, each doing the same kind of calculation. Instead of looping, we store all the layer's weights in a matrix W and write the whole layer in one line:

output = activation( W x input + b )

One matrix multiplication computes every neuron of the layer at the same time, and GPUs are built to do exactly this very fast. That is what makes training large networks practical.

Input x = (1, 2). Hidden neuron A has weights (0.5, -1) and bias 0.5; hidden neuron B has weights (1, 1) and bias 0; both use ReLU. The output neuron has weights (0.5, 0.2), bias 0.1 and sigmoid.

  • A: 0.5 x 1 + (-1) x 2 + 0.5 = -1, and ReLU(-1) = 0.
  • B: 1 x 1 + 1 x 2 + 0 = 3, and ReLU(3) = 3.
  • Output sum: 0.5 x 0 + 0.2 x 3 + 0.1 = 0.7. Sigmoid(0.7) = 0.668.

The prediction is 0.668. If the true answer is 1, the squared error is (1 - 0.668)^2 = 0.11. This error is what the next step, backpropagation, uses to improve the weights.

One layer has two neurons. The input is x = (3, 1). The weight matrix (table of weights) W has the rows (1, 2) and (0, -1). The biases are (0, 2). The layer uses ReLU.

Explanation

Each row of W belongs to one neuron.

Neuron 1: 1 x 3 + 2 x 1 + 0 = 5.

Neuron 2: 0 x 3 + (-1) x 1 + 2 = 1.

ReLU keeps positive numbers, so the output is (5, 1).

One matrix calculation does the sums for all neurons in the layer.

8.8Training a network: the big picture

Training turns a network with random weights into a useful one. It is the same idea as gradient descent from the previous chapter, applied to every weight in the network.

  1. Start with small random weights.
  2. Forward pass: compute the prediction for a batch of examples.
  3. Loss: compare the prediction with the true answer to get a single error number.
  4. Backward pass (backpropagation): work out how much each weight contributed to the error (its gradient).
  5. Update: change every weight slightly against its gradient.
  6. Repeat for all batches, for many epochs, until the loss is low.

In ANN terminology, the learning rule is gradient descent (how weights are changed) combined with backpropagation (how the gradients are computed efficiently).

Why not search for good weights at random? A network may have millions of weights, so the number of combinations is astronomical. Gradient descent tells every weight, at once, which direction to move.

A network has only 100 weights. Each weight can have one of 10 values.

Explanation

The first weight has 10 choices. Two weights have 10 x 10 = 100 choices.

For 100 weights, there are 10 to the power 100 choices. This is a 1 followed by 100 zeros.

A computer cannot try them all in any practical time.

Gradient descent does not try every choice. It uses the current error to find a direction for all weights together. It does not always find the best weights.

A very small network is: prediction = w x. The input is x = 1, the correct answer is 2, and w starts at 0.5.

Explanation

1. Forward pass: the prediction is 0.5 x 1 = 0.5.

2. Loss: (0.5 - 2) squared = 2.25.

3. Gradient (slope of the loss): 2 x (0.5 - 2) x 1 = -3.

4. Update with learning rate 0.1: w = 0.5 - 0.1 x (-3) = 0.8.

The new loss is (0.8 - 2) squared = 1.44. It is lower than before. A large network repeats the same four steps with many weights.

8.9Backpropagation

Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. For the output layer this is straightforward. But a weight deep inside the network affects the loss only indirectly, through all the layers after it. Backpropagation (short for "backward propagation of errors") is the efficient way to compute all these gradients.

The two passes

  1. Forward pass: input goes through the network to produce a prediction, and the loss is calculated.
  2. Backward pass: starting at the output layer, the algorithm uses the chain rule of calculus to work out how much each weight and bias contributed to the error, moving layer by layer toward the input.

The chain rule in everyday words

If a small change in weight A changes B, and a small change in B changes C, then the effect of A on C is (effect of A on B) multiplied by (effect of B on C). Backpropagation multiplies these effects along the path from the loss back to each weight. Each hidden neuron receives a share of the blame from the neurons it feeds, in proportion to the strength of its connections to them.

A tiny network with two weights in a row: h = w1 x and prediction = w2 h. Let x = 1, w1 = 2, w2 = 3 and the true answer y = 4. Loss = (prediction - y)^2.

  • Forward: h = 2, prediction = 6, loss = (6 - 4)^2 = 4.
  • Backward, output first: dLoss/dprediction = 2 x (6 - 4) = 4. Then dLoss/dw2 = 4 x h = 8.
  • Pass the blame back: dLoss/dh = 4 x w2 = 12. Then dLoss/dw1 = 12 x x = 12.
  • Update with learning rate 0.01: w2 = 3 - 0.01 x 8 = 2.92 and w1 = 2 - 0.01 x 12 = 1.88.
  • Check: new h = 1.88, new prediction = 2.92 x 1.88 = 5.49, new loss = 2.22. The loss fell from 4 to 2.22.

Notice that w1 never saw the loss directly; it received its gradient through w2, passed backward. That is backpropagation.

Why go backward? The gradient for an early layer needs the gradients of all later layers. Going from the output backward lets us compute each piece once and reuse it, so the whole backward pass costs about the same as one forward pass. Doing it forward, weight by weight, would be hopelessly slow.

A network has 1,000,000 weights. We need to know how each weight affects the loss.

Explanation

A slow method changes one weight a little and runs the network again. It must do this for every weight, so it needs about 1,000,000 extra forward passes for one update.

Backpropagation starts at the output. It calculates each shared part once and uses it again for earlier layers.

It needs one forward pass and one backward pass. The backward pass costs a similar order of work as the forward pass.

Updating the weights

Once backpropagation provides dL/dw for every weight, each is updated with the gradient descent rule: w_new = w_old - learning rate x dL/dw. This happens for all weights and biases in all layers at the end of each training step (for example, after each mini-batch).

A chain has three steps: h = 3w, then p = 2h, then loss = (p - 10) squared. We start with w = 1.

Explanation

Forward: h = 3, p = 6 and loss = 16.

Now go backward. A small change in p changes the loss -8 times as much.

A change in h changes p 2 times as much. A change in w changes h 3 times as much.

Multiply the three effects: -8 x 2 x 3 = -48. This is the gradient for w.

To test it, set w to 1.001. The loss becomes about 15.952. It falls by about 0.048, which matches -48 x 0.001.

8.10Convergence problems in training

Convergence means the loss settles at a low, stable value. Several things can prevent this.

ProblemWhat happensCommon remedies
Vanishing gradientsin deep networks the gradients shrink as they travel backward, so early layers barely change and learning stallsReLU activation, careful weight initialisation, LSTM, skip connections
Exploding gradientsgradients grow huge, weight updates become enormous and the loss turns into NaN (not a number)gradient clipping, a smaller learning rate
Poor hyperparameterslearning rate too high or low, bad initial weights, unsuitable optimisertune on the validation set
Local minima and plateausthe loss surface is bumpy, so training can settle in a poor valley or crawl across a flat regionmini-batch noise, momentum, the Adam optimiser
Hard data or weak modelthe loss stays high however you tunebetter data or a more suitable architecture

Why do gradients vanish? By the chain rule, the gradient reaching an early layer is a product of many numbers, one per layer. If each is less than 1 the product collapses. The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so ten sigmoid layers multiply to about 0.25 to the power 10, roughly 0.000001. The first layers receive almost no signal and cannot learn. ReLU has slope 1 for positive inputs, which is why it largely fixes the problem.

A message goes through four people. Each person keeps only 25 percent of its strength. The starting strength is 100.

Explanation

After each person, the strength is 25, then 6.25, then 1.56, then 0.39.

Almost nothing reaches the end of the line.

A gradient travels backward through layers in a similar way. The first layers are at the end of this path.

The slope of sigmoid is never above 0.25, so it can shrink the gradient quickly. Weights also affect the gradient. For positive inputs, the slope of ReLU is 1, so this slope does not shrink the gradient.

In a simple model, each layer multiplies the gradient by one number.

Case 1: multiply by 0.25 in each of 5 layers.

Case 2: multiply by 1.5 in each of 20 layers.

Explanation

Case 1 leaves about 0.001. The gradient is almost gone. This shows a vanishing gradient.

Case 2 gives about 3,300. The gradient is very large. This shows an exploding gradient.

The cause is repeated multiplication. In a real network, the number is different in each layer.

8.11Evaluating a network: reading the loss curves

While training we plot the loss against the number of epochs, for both the training data and the validation data. These two curves tell the whole story.

  • Healthy training: both curves fall and end up close together.
  • Overfitting: training loss keeps falling, but validation loss turns upward. The network is now memorising the training set rather than learning general patterns.
  • Underfitting: both curves stay high; the network is too weak or training was too short.

Remedies for overfitting: early stopping (stop at the epoch where validation loss is lowest), more data, dropout, regularisation, or a smaller network.

These losses are made up. We record them after 10, 20, 30 and 40 epochs.

Training loss: 0.60, 0.40, 0.28, 0.20.

Validation loss: 0.65, 0.48, 0.45, 0.55.

Explanation

Up to epoch 30, both losses go down. The model gets better.

At epoch 40, the training loss is lower, but the validation loss is higher. This is a sign of overfitting.

Of these four points, keep the model from epoch 30. Real results go up and down, so wait for several worse results before you stop.

8.12Exam questions and model answers: Chapter 8

Q1. Compare a biological neuron with an artificial neuron.

A biological neuron receives signals through dendrites, sums them in the cell body, fires along the axon if a threshold is reached, and the strength of each synapse changes with learning. An artificial neuron receives numerical inputs, multiplies each by a weight (the synapse strength), adds a bias, and passes the sum through an activation function to give its output. The biological neuron is vastly more complex; about 86 billion neurons in the brain compared with a simple mathematical function in an ANN.

Q2. Describe the structure of an Artificial Neural Network.

An ANN has an input layer with one node per feature (no computation), one or more hidden layers that learn complex patterns (more than one makes it "deep"), and an output layer that gives the prediction; its size and activation depend on the task. Every connection carries a weight and every neuron a bias; these are the learnable parameters.

Q3. What is the significance of activation functions?

They introduce non-linearity. Without them any number of layers would be equivalent to a single linear model, so the network could not learn complex patterns. They also set the range of a neuron's output. Sigmoid gives 0 to 1 (probabilities), tanh gives -1 to 1, and ReLU gives max(0, z) and is the default for hidden layers because it is cheap and reduces vanishing gradients.

Q4. What are the effects of weights and bias?

A weight sets the strength and sign of an input's influence: large positive means strong excitation, negative means inhibition, near zero means little effect. The bias is a constant added to the weighted sum that shifts the activation function left or right, like the intercept in y = mx + c; without it the neuron's boundary would always pass through the origin.

Q5. What are the learning rules in an ANN?

The standard learning rule is gradient descent combined with backpropagation. Gradient descent adjusts the weights in the direction that reduces the loss most steeply; backpropagation efficiently computes the gradient of the loss for every weight by passing the error backward through the network.

Q6. What is forward propagation?

The process of computing the network's output for a given input by passing data layer by layer from the input to the output. At each layer, each neuron computes the weighted sum of its inputs plus bias and applies the activation function; the results become the next layer's inputs.

Q7. Describe the backpropagation algorithm and explain how the error propagates backward.

Backpropagation trains multi-layer networks in two phases. The forward pass computes the prediction and the loss. In the backward pass, starting at the output layer, the chain rule is applied to compute the partial derivative of the loss with respect to each weight and bias, layer by layer toward the input. Each hidden neuron receives a share of the error from the neurons it connects to, weighted by the connection strengths. These gradients are then used to update the weights.

Q8. How are weights updated in a multi-layer network?

After backpropagation gives dL/dw for each weight, every weight is updated using w_new = w_old - learning rate x dL/dw, for all weights and biases across all layers, typically at the end of each mini-batch.

Q9. What are the common convergence issues in training neural networks?

Vanishing gradients (early layers stop learning), exploding gradients (unstable, huge updates and NaN loss), poor hyperparameter choices such as the learning rate and initialisation, getting stuck in local minima or plateaus, and difficult data or an inadequate architecture.

Q10. Why is matrix multiplication fundamental in neural networks?

The weighted sums of all neurons in a layer can be computed with one matrix-vector multiplication, output = activation(W x input + b), which GPUs execute extremely fast in parallel. This makes training deep networks feasible.

Q11. What is the significance of the dot product in a neuron?

The dot product of the weight vector and the input vector is exactly the weighted sum inside a neuron. It also measures how similar two vectors are, which is used in many other methods.

Chapter 9

Specialised Networks: CNN, RNN and LSTM

Architectures designed for images and for sequences.

9.1Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)

A CNN is a network designed for images (and other grid-like data such as video frames and medical scans).

Why not just use an ordinary network for pictures?

A small 224 by 224 colour photo has 224 x 224 x 3 = 150,528 numbers. One hidden layer of 1,000 neurons connected to every pixel would need over 150 million weights. That is wasteful, and it ignores the most important property of images: nearby pixels belong together, and a feature such as an edge looks the same wherever it appears. A CNN uses this structure.

The building blocks

  • Convolution layer. A small grid of weights called a filter (or kernel), for example 3 x 3, slides across the image. At each position it multiplies its weights with the pixels beneath it and adds them up, producing one number. The collection of these numbers is a feature map showing where in the image that pattern (an edge, a corner, a texture) was found. The same filter is reused at every position, so the layer needs only a handful of weights and detects the pattern anywhere in the picture. The filter values are learned during training.
  • Activation (ReLU) is applied after convolution to add non-linearity.
  • Pooling layer. Shrinks each feature map, for example by keeping only the maximum of each 2 x 2 block (max pooling). This cuts computation and makes the network tolerant to small shifts of the object in the picture.
  • Flatten and fully connected layers. The final feature maps are laid out as a list and passed to ordinary layers that make the final decision, such as "cat" or "dog".

Early convolution layers find simple features (edges), later ones combine them into parts (eyes, wheels), and the last ones into whole objects. This is the "hierarchy of features" idea behind deep learning.

An image has 28 x 28 pixels and only gray shades. So it has 784 input values. We count the parameters of two layers.

A dense layer (every neuron sees every pixel) has 100 neurons.

A convolution layer has 32 filters of size 3 x 3.

Explanation

Dense layer: 784 x 100 weights + 100 biases = 78,500.

Convolution layer: each filter has 9 weights and 1 bias. So 32 x 10 = 320.

A filter uses the same weights at every place in the image. This is why the number is small.

The two layers give outputs of different sizes. The example compares only how they use weights.

9.2Worked example: convolution and pooling by hand

Convolution

A 4 x 4 image: bright (9) on the left, dark (0) on the right, so there is a vertical edge in the middle.

9 9 0 0
9 9 0 0
9 9 0 0
9 9 0 0

A 2 x 2 filter, which compares the left column with the right column:

 1 -1
 1 -1

Slide it across, multiplying pairs and adding:

  • Left position: 9x1 + 9x(-1) + 9x1 + 9x(-1) = 0 (both columns equally bright)
  • Middle position: 9x1 + 0x(-1) + 9x1 + 0x(-1) = 18 (bright on the left, dark on the right: an edge)
  • Right position: 0 (both dark)

Every row of the output is 0, 18, 0. The large value marks exactly where the edge is.

Max pooling (2 x 2)

1 3 | 2 1
4 6 | 5 2
----+----
3 1 | 0 7
2 8 | 9 4

Keep the largest number in each block:

6 5
8 9

The 4 x 4 map became 2 x 2, a quarter of the size, and the strongest responses survived.

Why max? We care whether the feature was detected somewhere in the block, not its exact position. That is what gives tolerance to small movements.

We want to find a horizontal edge.

The image rows are (5 5 5), (5 5 5) and (1 1 1).

The filter rows are (1 1) and (-1 -1).

Explanation

The filter adds two upper pixels and subtracts the two pixels below them.

On image rows 1 and 2: 5 + 5 - 5 - 5 = 0. The brightness does not change.

On image rows 2 and 3: 5 + 5 - 1 - 1 = 8. Here the brightness changes, so there is an edge.

The filter moves left to right too. The full result has the rows (0, 0) and (8, 8).

9.3Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)

Some data comes in a sequence where order matters: sentences, speech, stock prices over time. The word "bank" means different things in "river bank" and "bank loan"; the meaning depends on the words around it. An ordinary network treats every input separately and has no memory, so it cannot use this context.

An RNN adds memory. It reads the sequence one step at a time. At each step it combines the new input x with its hidden state h, which summarises everything seen so far, to produce a new hidden state. The same weights are used at every step, so the network can handle sequences of any length.

The vanishing gradient problem in RNNs

To learn, the error must be passed backward through every time step (backpropagation through time). At each step the gradient is multiplied again by a number that is usually below 1, so after many steps it becomes almost zero. The RNN then cannot link something that happened long ago to something happening now. In "The cat, which had been sitting on the warm mat all afternoon, was hungry", a plain RNN has trouble remembering that the subject is "cat" by the time it reaches "was". It effectively forgets early inputs.

A very small RNN has one memory number, h. The rule is: new h = 0.5 x old h + input. At the start, h = 0.

Sequence A is 1, then 0. Sequence B is 0, then 1.

Explanation

Sequence A: h becomes 1, then 0.5.

Sequence B: h becomes 0, then 1.

Both sequences use the same numbers, but the final memory is different. So the order matters.

If sequence A gets one more 0, h falls to 0.25. The old input fades. A real RNN is more complex and learns its weights.

9.4Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)

The LSTM is a special RNN designed to fix the vanishing gradient problem and remember over long spans.

The idea: give the network a separate long-term memory, the cell state, which passes along the sequence with only small, controlled changes. Three gates control it. Each gate is a small neural unit that outputs a number between 0 (block everything) and 1 (let everything through).

GateDecides
Forget gatewhich information from the old cell state to discard and which to keep
Input gatewhich new information from the current input to write into the cell state
Output gatewhich part of the cell state to send out as the hidden state for the next step

Analogy: a notebook. The forget gate erases notes that are no longer useful, the input gate writes down what is important from today, and the output gate decides which notes to read out right now.

Why does the LSTM remember better? The cell state is mostly passed along unchanged, controlled by gates close to 1. Because information travels almost unchanged, the gradient can also flow backward over many steps without shrinking to nothing. That is how it solves the vanishing gradient problem.

We pass a memory value through 100 steps.

Case 1: keep 99 percent at each step.

Case 2: keep 50 percent at each step.

Explanation

In case 1, about 37 percent remains.

In case 2, the part that remains is almost zero.

When the forget gate is close to 1, the LSTM keeps most of the memory. The gradient on the same memory path also shrinks slowly.

The LSTM learns when to keep or forget. It reduces the vanishing gradient problem, but very long sequences can still be hard.

We follow one memory value through one LSTM step. The old memory is 10. The new candidate value is 4. The forget gate is 0.9, and the input gate is 0.5.

Explanation

The forget gate keeps 90 percent of the old memory: 0.9 x 10 = 9.

The input gate adds 50 percent of the new value: 0.5 x 4 = 2.

The new memory is 9 + 2 = 11.

The output gate controls what the cell shows. The cell first applies tanh, and tanh(11) is almost 1. With an output gate of 0.2, the output is about 0.2.

So the cell can store 11 but send out only a small value.

9.5Choosing the right network

NetworkBest forKey ideaExample
Feed-forward (ANN)tables of featureslayers of weighted sums and activationsloan approval, fraud detection
CNNimages, videoshared sliding filters and poolingface recognition, reading X-rays
RNNshort sequences, time serieshidden state acts as memorysensor readings, simple text
LSTMlong sequencesgates control a long-term memorytranslation, speech recognition
Transformerlanguage and moreattention: look directly at the relevant parts of the inputChatGPT-style assistants

Choose a network for each job:

1. Predict loan risk from a table with 12 columns.

2. Find a crack in a photo of a wall.

3. Predict the next sensor value from the last 10 values.

4. Translate a long paragraph.

Explanation

Good first choices are: feed-forward network for job 1, CNN for job 2, RNN for job 3 and Transformer for job 4.

The shape of the data guides the choice: a table, an image, a short sequence, or long text.

An LSTM can also do jobs 3 and 4. Today, Transformers are the usual choice for translation. For job 1, also compare a simpler ML model.

9.6Exam questions and model answers: Chapter 9

Q1. What is a CNN and where is it used? Explain convolution and pooling.

A Convolutional Neural Network is designed for image data. Convolution layers slide small filters (kernels) over the image to detect local features such as edges, corners and textures, producing feature maps; the same filter is reused across the image, which keeps the number of weights small. Pooling layers, for example max pooling, down-sample the feature maps, reducing dimensions and computation and making the model robust to small shifts of the object. CNNs are used for image classification, object detection and face recognition.

Q2. Why is a CNN preferred to an ordinary neural network for images?

An ordinary network would need a huge number of weights (millions per layer for a normal photo) and ignores the spatial structure of images. A CNN exploits local patterns and reuses filters, so it needs far fewer parameters and detects a feature wherever it appears.

Q3. What is an RNN? What is the vanishing gradient problem?

A Recurrent Neural Network processes sequential data step by step and keeps a hidden state that acts as memory of earlier inputs, so it suits text, speech and time series. The vanishing gradient problem occurs when gradients, propagated backward through many time steps, are repeatedly multiplied by small values and shrink toward zero; the network then forgets early inputs and cannot learn long-range dependencies.

Q4. How does LSTM solve the vanishing gradient problem?

An LSTM has a cell state that carries information along the sequence with minimal change, regulated by three gates. The forget gate discards unneeded information, the input gate stores new useful information, and the output gate chooses what to pass on as the hidden state. Because the cell state is largely preserved, gradients can flow back across many time steps without vanishing.

Q5. Name the key applications of deep learning.

Computer vision (image classification, object detection, face recognition) with CNNs; natural language processing (translation, sentiment analysis, chatbots) with RNNs, LSTMs and Transformers; and predictive analytics (stock forecasting, fraud detection, disease diagnosis).

Q6. Write the convolution of the image rows 9 9 0 0 (four identical rows) with the filter [1 -1; 1 -1].

Sliding the 2 x 2 filter gives 9(1) + 9(-1) + 9(1) + 9(-1) = 0 at the left, 9 - 0 + 9 - 0 = 18 in the middle, and 0 at the right, so each output row is 0, 18, 0. The high value marks the vertical edge between the bright and dark regions.

Revision Guide and Exam Preparation

Definitions, formulas, comparisons and answer-writing technique, plus the perceptron learning algorithm.

10.1The perceptron learning algorithm (logic of the program)

This is a frequently asked "write the logic" question. The perceptron learns by correcting its own mistakes.

  1. Initialise: set every weight to zero or a small random number, set the bias to 0, and choose a small learning rate such as 0.1.
  2. Loop over the training examples, for a fixed number of epochs or until no mistakes are made. For each example (inputs x, true label y):
    1. Calculate the sum: w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + bias.
    2. Apply the step function: predict 1 if the sum is greater than 0, otherwise 0.
    3. Calculate the error: error = y - prediction.
    4. If error is not zero, update: each weight w = w + learning rate x error x x, and bias = bias + learning rate x error.
  3. Predict new data with the final weights and bias, using steps (a) and (b).

Why does the update fix the mistake? If the neuron predicted 0 but the answer was 1, the error is +1, so the weights of the active inputs increase and the sum is larger next time, pushing the output toward 1. If it predicted 1 but the answer was 0, the error is -1, the weights decrease and the sum falls. When the prediction is right the error is 0 and nothing changes.

The perceptron has weights (-1, 0) and bias 0. The learning rate is 0.5. The input is (1, 1), and the correct answer is 1.

Explanation

The sum is -1, so the prediction is 0. The sum is too low.

Error = 1 - 0 = +1.

The new weights are (-0.5, 0.5), and the new bias is 0.5.

The new sum is -0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 0.5. The sum is above 0, so the prediction is now 1.

The update raised the sum for this input. This moved the output toward the correct answer.

Weights (0, 0), bias 0, learning rate 1. Example: x = (1, 1) with label y = 1. Sum = 0, so the prediction is 0 and the error is 1. Update: weights become (0 + 1x1x1, 0 + 1x1x1) = (1, 1) and the bias becomes 0 + 1x1 = 1. Check: the new sum is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, which gives prediction 1. Correct.

The perceptron is guaranteed to find a solution only if the classes can be separated by a straight line. That is why it fails on XOR and why multi-layer networks with backpropagation were needed.

The perceptron has weights (1, 1) and bias 0. The learning rate is 0.5. The input is (1, 0), and the correct answer is 0.

Explanation

The sum is 1, so the prediction is 1. This is wrong.

Error = correct answer - prediction = 0 - 1 = -1.

The new weights are (0.5, 1), and the new bias is -0.5.

The new sum is 0. The rule gives 1 only for a sum above 0, so the prediction is now 0.

The second weight stays the same, because its input is 0. Sometimes one update is not enough.

10.5How to write a strong exam answer

  1. Start with a one-line definition in your own words.
  2. Give the reason: why does this exist, or what problem does it solve? This is where most marks are won.
  3. Add an example: a spam filter, house price prediction, cancer screening. A concrete example shows understanding.
  4. Draw the diagram when one exists: the nested AI-ML-DL circles, the confusion matrix, the gradient descent valley, the overfitting curves, the neural network layers, the workflow boxes.
  5. For "compare" questions use a table with four or five rows.
  6. For "write the logic" questions give numbered steps first (initialise, loop, update, stop).
  7. For numerical questions write the formula, substitute the numbers, and state the final value.

10.6Self-test: try these without looking

1. Draw the relationship between AI, ML, DL and Data Science.

AI is the outermost region, ML sits inside AI, and Deep Learning sits inside ML. Data Science is drawn as an overlapping region because it uses ML and statistics as tools to extract insight from data.

2. A model has 99 percent training accuracy and 70 percent test accuracy. What is wrong, and what can you do?

It is overfitting: it has memorised the training data but does not generalise. Remedies are more data, a simpler model or fewer features, regularisation, cross-validation, early stopping, and dropout (in neural networks).

3. Why do we keep a test set that is never used during training?

So that we obtain an honest, unbiased estimate of how the model performs on new data. If the test data influenced training or tuning, the score would be optimistic because of data leakage.

4. Why do we subtract the gradient instead of adding it?

The gradient points in the direction in which the loss increases fastest. To reduce the loss we must move the opposite way, so we subtract it.

5. What happens if the learning rate is too large? Too small?

Too large: the steps overshoot the minimum, the loss oscillates or even grows (divergence). Too small: learning is very slow and may stall before reaching a good solution.

6. Why is a non-linear activation function necessary?

Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear transformation, so the network could only learn straight-line relationships. Non-linearity lets it learn curved, complex patterns such as XOR.

7. Explain the forward pass and the backward pass in your own words.

The forward pass pushes the input through the layers to produce a prediction and compute the loss. The backward pass sends the error back from the output toward the input, using the chain rule to find how much each weight contributed to the error; the weights are then adjusted to reduce it.

8. What does pooling do, and why?

It reduces the size of feature maps (for example keeping the maximum in each block). This lowers computation and makes the network less sensitive to the exact position of a feature.

9. Why does an LSTM remember longer than a plain RNN?

Its cell state is passed along the sequence with little change, controlled by forget, input and output gates, so information and gradients survive across many time steps instead of vanishing.

10. A classifier gives TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30. Find accuracy, precision, recall and F1.

Accuracy = 70/100 = 0.70; precision = 40/50 = 0.80; recall = 40/60 = 0.667; F1 = 2 x 0.8 x 0.667 / (0.8 + 0.667) = 0.727.
